summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\), one of \((11,13),(7,19),(5,29),(3,17),(2,17)\) consists of two primes not dividing \(d\); each pair has distinct final digits and product at most \(150\). Since \(d\) is then invertible modulo that product, some \(0\le i<pq\le150\) makes \(a+id\) divisible by both primes, so that term has prime divisors with different final digits.

full_proof.text:
We prove that no such arithmetic progression exists.

Call an integer \(n>1\) lopsided if all prime divisors of \(n\) have the same residue modulo \(10\), equivalently, if their final decimal digits are all the same. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers \(a,d\) such that
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025,
\]
and every one of
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
is lopsided.

We first establish a modular observation that will be used repeatedly.

**Modular observation.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be distinct primes such that
\[
p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d,\qquad pq\le 150.
\]
Then one of the first \(150\) terms \(a+id\), with \(0\le i<150\), is divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\).

Indeed, because \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Consequently \(d\) has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(pq\). If \(e\) is such an inverse, choose \(i\) to be the unique integer satisfying
\[
0\le i<pq,\qquad i\equiv -ae\pmod{pq}.
\]
Then
\[
a+id\equiv a+(-ae)d\equiv a-a\equiv 0\pmod{pq}.
\]
Thus \(pq\mid a+id\). Since \(i<pq\le150\), this index is one of \(0,1,\ldots,149\), as required.

In particular, if the final decimal digits of \(p\) and \(q\) are different, then this term cannot be lopsided: it is at least \(a\ge2\), and both \(p\) and \(q\) are among its prime divisors, while \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\).

We now show that every possible difference \(d\) with \(1\le d\le2025\) admits a pair \((p,q)\) to which this observation applies. Consider the following five pairs of primes:
\[
(11,13),\quad (7,19),\quad (5,29),\quad (3,17),\quad (2,17).
\]
We claim that for at least one of these pairs, neither prime divides \(d\). In other words, at least one of the following five alternatives holds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&11\nmid d\text{ and }13\nmid d,\\
&7\nmid d\text{ and }19\nmid d,\\
&5\nmid d\text{ and }29\nmid d,\\
&3\nmid d\text{ and }17\nmid d,\\
&2\nmid d\text{ and }17\nmid d.
\end{aligned}
\]

Suppose the claim were false. Then each pair would contain at least one prime dividing \(d\). In particular,
\[
11\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d,
\]
\[
7\mid d\text{ or }19\mid d,
\]
and
\[
5\mid d\text{ or }29\mid d.
\]
We split into two cases according to whether \(17\) divides \(d\).

First suppose \(17\mid d\). Choose
\[
r\in\{11,13\},\qquad s\in\{7,19\},\qquad t\in\{5,29\}
\]
so that \(r\mid d\), \(s\mid d\), and \(t\mid d\); such choices exist by the preceding three disjunctions. The four numbers \(r,s,t,17\) are distinct primes. Hence they are pairwise coprime, and their product divides \(d\):
\[
rst\cdot17\mid d.
\]
As \(d\ge1\), this implies
\[
d\ge rst\cdot17\ge 11\cdot7\cdot5\cdot17=6545,
\]
contradicting \(d\le2025\).

Now suppose \(17\nmid d\). Since the pair \((3,17)\) was assumed to contain a divisor of \(d\), it follows that \(3\mid d\). Similarly, the pair \((2,17)\) forces \(2\mid d\). Again choose divisors
\[
r\in\{11,13\},\qquad s\in\{7,19\},\qquad t\in\{5,29\}
\]
of \(d\). The five primes \(r,s,t,3,2\) are distinct, so their product divides \(d\). Therefore
\[
d\ge rst\cdot3\cdot2
   \ge 11\cdot7\cdot5\cdot3\cdot2
   =2310,
\]
again contradicting \(d\le2025\).

Both cases are impossible. Thus at least one of the five displayed pairs consists entirely of primes not dividing \(d\).

It remains to check that each possible pair has the two other properties required in the modular observation: its product is at most \(150\), and its two primes have different final digits. These checks are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(p,q)&pq&(p\bmod10,q\bmod10)\\ \hline
(11,13)&143&(1,3)\\
(7,19)&133&(7,9)\\
(5,29)&145&(5,9)\\
(3,17)&51&(3,7)\\
(2,17)&34&(2,7).
\end{array}
\]
Every product in the middle column is at most \(150\), and the two residues in every entry of the last column are unequal.

Choose the pair supplied by the divisibility argument. Since neither member divides \(d\), the modular observation gives an index \(i\) with \(0\le i<150\) for which
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]
Thus both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime divisors of \(a+id\). Their final decimal digits differ, so \(a+id\) is not lopsided. This contradicts the assumption that all \(150\) terms of the progression are lopsided.

Therefore there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) such that every term \(a+id\), for \(0\le i<150\), belongs to A381159.
